+# Job Worker Service
+
+## What
+
+A prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Details
+
+### High-level design
+
+![high-level design](assets/jws.jpg)
+
+To build our service with scalability in mind, we would need to design the service in such a way that makes it possible to scale every component in our service separately
+
+#### Control Plane
+
+Control plane will represent our customer facing API, which can either be an API GW, or a load balancer, and a cluster of containers behind it to process client requests. This control plane will be responsible for the following tasks:
+
+- Provide an API for data plane agents to register: agents will be installed and started on a fleet of hosts in data plane. They will need to register themselves with our control plane using a pre-configured api key.
+- Monitor the registered agents with heartbeats: Upon registering an agent in our control plane, the agent will start sending heartbeats to the control plane over a specific interval to allow making decision as to when our control plane should backoff on sending traffic to the agent if/when it's busy. These heartbeats can also be used to monitor the state of the jobs that the agent has been assigned.
+- Authenticate clients and process job requests: Once a client request is authenticated in our control plane using mTLS, the request will be routed by our control plane to an appropriate agent for execution.
+- Add a record about the job in a persistent external datastore: After re-routing the job to an agent, control plane will insert a record to a datastore (such as DynamoDB). This record will include metadata about the job that's being executed, the identifier of the agent that it was assigned to, and the state of the job.
+- Update the state of the job in the datastore: based on the heartbeats received from the agent, our control plane will update the state of the jobs that the agent was assigned accordingly.
+
+This persistent datastore will allow any container in our control plane cluster to respond to client requests belonging to any job and idenfiy which agent the job is running on when needed, as well as handling service restarts.
+
+#### Data Plane
+
+Data plane will consist of fleet of hosts that will be managed by an agent. Ideally, this fleet can be owned and provided by the client themself in case of sophisticated systems with high traffic, especially where multi-tenancy is not an option. Though a limited service fleet can be built to accommodate simple client requests. The agent will expose an internal API which should only be accessible by our control plane. This API will be used by our control plane to submit new jobs to the agent, query, or request the output stream of any given job. Agent will track the jobs that it has been assigned in memory.
+
+### Security
+
+The reason to separate out the execution environment (where the jobs are executed) from the rest of our service components is not just to achieve scalability, but also because - and due to the nature of our service - this execution environment is meant to be an untrusted environment. That means, the execution environment needs to be an isolated environment that doesn't handle any credentials or sensitive information, and is not allowed access to any other components in our service or infrastructure.
+
+Other general security considerations include:
+- All client-server and inter-service communications are sent over TLS.
+- A basic client authn/authz scheme is implemented over mTLS.
+- TLSv1.3 is used with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 cipher.
+- Resource isolation will be implemented to make sure each job is executed in a separate Pid namespace, network namespace and mount namespace.
+- Control groups will be used to control how much resource each job can access.
+
+A future improvement could be to implement a seccomp filter and limit access to the kernel and syscalls that a job can make. Linux capabilities can also be used to control what capabilities any job/process will have.
+
+### Scope
+
+As the purpose of this project is to prototype our service only, we are going to limit the scope to include only the data plane agent in standalone mode, where it will be possible to send the requests directly to the agent's API, and the agent will handle the client authn/authz instead. The implementation of this agent is going to be broken down into 3 components:
+
+- A reusable library implementing the functionality for working with jobs.
+- An API server that wraps the functionality of the library.
+- A command line interface (CLI) that communicates with the API server.
+
+### Protobuf Definition
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+option go_package = "github.com/p4n1c/jws/internal/pb";
+
+message StartRequest {
+  // Path to the command to run.
+  string cmd = 1;
+
+  // Arguments to pass to the command, if any.
+  repeated string args = 2;
+}
+
+message StartResponse {
+  // Server assigned id for the started job.
+  string job_id = 1;
+}
+
+message StopRequest {
+  // Server assigned id previously returned in response to a Start call.
+  string job_id = 1;

+message StopResponse {
+  // nothing to return in successful case.
+}
+
+message GetStatusRequest {
+  // Server assigned id previously returned in response to a Start call.
+  string job_id = 1;
+
+  bool is_detailed = 2;

+# Job Worker Service
+
+## What
+
+A prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Details
+
+### Scope
+
+We will implement a grpc API server with a backend library that allows clients to execute arbitrary Linux processes on a remote host. Our API server will expose the following API endpoints /Start, /Stop, /Query, and /Stream which are going to allow clients to start a process, stop a process, query to status of a process, and request the output stream of a process. Our project can be broken down into 3 components:
+
+- A reusable library implementing the functionality for working with jobs.
+- An API server that wraps the functionality of the library.
+- A command line interface (CLI) that communicates with the API server.
+
+### Library
+
+Our backend library will expose an interface that allows our API server to interact with the library and perform actions that correspond to each API endpoint. The implemented interface will be portable and will not be tied to our grpc server use-case, allowing other programs which might be looking to adapt any of the existing functionality to integrate easily with the library.
+
+#### Executor
+Executor is the main component in our library which will be responsible for the core business logic of executing, stopping, tracking the status, and streaming output of a process.
+
+##### Start Job
+For every new job started by Executor, a unique job identifier (a uuid string) will be generated which can be used by users of the library to perform actions on that particular job referencing its id. Following the generation of the job id, we will create a separate control group for the new job, execute the provided command and add the process id to the created control group. Executor will make sure that every command is executed in its own separate pid, network and mount namespaces.
+
+In order to make sure the process is executed in an isolated and controlled environment from the get-go, the execution flow for each job will involve the following steps:
+- **Control group creation:** We will create a cgroup for the job, we are going to have a 1:1 mapping between the cgroup and job, and make sure it has cpu, cpuset, memory and io controllers enabled, at this step the created cgroup will have no processes in it.
+- **Entrypoint execution:** We are going to implement a simple cmd ```entrypoint``` which will make sure that the provided command is executed inside an isolated environment. A pid, network, and mount namespaces will be initialized as part of this step by passing syscall.CLONE_NEWPID, syscall.CLONE_NEWNET and syscall.CLONE_NEWNS Cloneflags to the SysProcAttr of the initialized entrypoint's ```exec.Cmd``` object. It will also add itself to the job's specific cgroup which we have created in the previous step by also passing UseCgroupFD and CgroupFD to the SysProcAttr. The main purpose of this entrypoint cmd is to prepare a pivot root inside the new mount namespace which the job or the command provided will be executed in before it proceeds to executing the job's command.
+- **Job execution:** we will pass the provided command along with its arguments to our entrypoint script which will subsequently execute the command after it has completed preparing the isolated environment. The job's command will be then executed using ```syscall.Exec``` to replace the current process with the command itself allowing the new process to become the init inside our pid namespace.
+- **Record job information:** Once the command is executed successfully, Executor will add an entry to an in-memory map while holding a mutex to ensure safety. This map maintains information about every job it's executed, where the key of this map the job id, and the value is a job metadata model that will hold the information represented below.
+- **Wait for job to complete or exit:** Executor and after it has stored the job information in the in-memory map, it will call ```Wait()``` on the started command in order to wait for the process to exit.
+
+```
+type JobState int
+
+const (
+  // Job is running.
+  Running JobState = iota
+  // Job has been stopped by user through a Stop call.
+  Stopped
+  // Job has exited unexpectedly (for example due to invalid args, or permission denined while accessing a resource).
+  Exited
+  // Job has been terminated by service (likely due to OOMKiller).
+  Terminated
+)
+
+// Job status metadata including the process id, exit code if process exited, execution start time, execution end time and flags to indicate whether the process was terminated, and/or whether it is still running.
+type JobStatus struct {
+  Pid int
+  ExitCode int
+  StartTime time.Time
+  EndTime time.Time
+  State JobState
+}
+
+// Job metadata model which holds information about owner, actual command and job status.
+type Job struct {
+  Owner          string
+  JobID          string
+  Command        string
+  Args           []string
+  Cmd            *exec.Cmd
+  StdoutBuffer   OutputStream
+  StderrBuffer   OutputStream
+  CombinedBuffer OutputStream
+  Status         *JobStatus
+}
+```
+Note: the model is illustrative and might change slightly as the implementation evolves. 
+
+##### Stop Job
+
+Once a call is made to Executor to stop a job, it will validate the existence and the state of the job that's requested to be stopped, if the job doesn't exist we will return an error while if it's not running we will return a successful response. If the job exists and is in running state, then Executor will proceed to kill the job by interacting with the cgroup module to call ```KillJob()``` method which will utilizing the kill file feature from cgroups to kill all the processes running within the cgroup. After the job is killed successfully we will verify all the resources created for that job are throughly cleaned up and no resource is leaked or left behind. The other option would be to kill the process directly through the cmd object we are maintaining in our job metdata model which is equally going to SIGKILL the process. Though, using the cgroup method is going to be cleaner and easier especially when the job we are executing might start child processes, as that would require extra handling that we don't have to worry about with the ```cgroup.kill``` option.
+
+After stopping the job, Executor will still retain the job metadata information of the job but will discard the buffers that we have allocated for stdout, stderr through calling ```Close()``` on these buffers. It will also update the status of the job to indicate the job has been killed, and return the response to the client.
+
+Similarly during the service shutdown, it will be possible to kill all the running jobs by using the cgroup.kill file on the service/parent cgroup.
+
+##### Job Output Streaming
+
+During the execution of the job, Executor will initialize two memory buffers and redirect stdout and stderr of the process to the two buffers respectively, where a reference to those buffers will be maintained as part of the job metadata model in the in-memory map. Callers to the Executor's StreamOutput method will have initialize a channel and pass to the Executor in the input, and upon making a call to stream the output, we will initialize an outputStream object which will receive the requested memory buffer and the channel that the Caller passed in the input. This outputStream will be responsible for reading the content from the selected output buffer (whether that's stdout or stderr), and write the content of the buffer to the supplied channel. Caller (which is our API server in this case) will then read the data from the channel, and pass it over to the client using the grpc ```Send```. Output buffer will be implemented with mutex to ensure safety, it will also implement a mechanism to monitor the state of the buffer and block until new data to be written to the buffer or the buffer is closed.
+
+```
+// OutputStream is an interface representing a buffer implementation
+// that can store stdout, stderr and stream them out.
+type OutputStream interface {
+  sio.WriteCloser
+  sio.ReaderAt
+
+  Stream(dataChan chan []byte) error
+}
+
+// OutputBufferStream implements OutputStream.
+// It will hold output of the job/process being executed and Stream it when requested.
+type OutputBufferStream struct {
+  // internal buffer to hold the actual process output
+  buf      []byte
+  // closed is a boolean to indicate that buffer is closed
+  closed   bool
+  // mutex to ensure access safety.
+  *sync.RWMutex
+}
+```
+
+#### Control groups
+
+cgroup is the second core module in our library which will provide a wrapper around multiple cgroups v2 features, the module will be implemented to be self-contained and can be used separately from the rest of the library core modules. 
+
+During the initialization of an Executor instance, it will interact with the cgroup module to make sure the requested controllers/subsystems are supported and enabled, then it will create a parent control group ```/sys/fs/cgroup/jws```, that will later hold the per-job child cgroups, so our hierarchy will look like:
+
+          ($root cgroup - /sys/fs/cgroup)
+                         |
+                         |
+           ($service cgroup - $root/jws)
+            /            |            \
+           /             |             \
+    ($service/job1) ($service/job2) ($server/job3) ...
+
+This hierarchy will allow us to control job's access to the resources in two ways, the first is by setting an upper limit for our different resources on the parent/service cgroup and let the different jobs compete for the resources depending on their need. While the second way is by limiting the job itself if the need arise.
+
+For simplicity we will cover only the following controls:
+- **Cpu:** we will support setting cpu time quota in ```cpu.max``` during one period.
+- **Memory:** we will support setting ```memory.high``` to throttle process's usage, and ```memory.max``` to set the upper boundry for which the process will OOMKilled if exceeded.
+- **Io:** we will support setting rbps and wbps in ```io.max```

+Executor is the main component in our library which will be responsible for the core business logic of executing, stopping, tracking the status, and streaming output of a process.
+
+##### Start Job
+For every new job started by Executor, a unique job identifier (a uuid string) will be generated which can be used by users of the library to perform actions on that particular job referencing its id. Following the generation of the job id, we will create a separate control group for the new job, execute the provided command and add the process id to the created control group. Executor will make sure that every command is executed in its own separate pid, network and mount namespaces.
+
+In order to make sure the process is executed in an isolated and controlled environment from the get-go, the execution flow for each job will involve the following steps:
+- **Control group creation:** We will create a cgroup for the job, we are going to have a 1:1 mapping between the cgroup and job, and make sure it has cpu, cpuset, memory and io controllers enabled, at this step the created cgroup will have no processes in it.
+- **Entrypoint execution:** We are going to implement a simple cmd ```entrypoint``` which will make sure that the provided command is executed inside an isolated environment. A pid, network, and mount namespaces will be initialized as part of this step by passing syscall.CLONE_NEWPID, syscall.CLONE_NEWNET and syscall.CLONE_NEWNS Cloneflags to the SysProcAttr of the initialized entrypoint's ```exec.Cmd``` object. It will also add itself to the job's specific cgroup which we have created in the previous step by also passing UseCgroupFD and CgroupFD to the SysProcAttr. The main purpose of this entrypoint cmd is to prepare a pivot root inside the new mount namespace which the job or the command provided will be executed in before it proceeds to executing the job's command.
+- **Job execution:** we will pass the provided command along with its arguments to our entrypoint script which will subsequently execute the command after it has completed preparing the isolated environment. The job's command will be then executed using ```syscall.Exec``` to replace the current process with the command itself allowing the new process to become the init inside our pid namespace.
+- **Record job information:** Once the command is executed successfully, Executor will add an entry to an in-memory map while holding a mutex to ensure safety. This map maintains information about every job it's executed, where the key of this map the job id, and the value is a job metadata model that will hold the information represented below.
+- **Wait for job to complete or exit:** Executor and after it has stored the job information in the in-memory map, it will call ```Wait()``` on the started command in order to wait for the process to exit.
+
+```
+type JobState int
+
+const (
+  // Job is running.
+  Running JobState = iota
+  // Job has been stopped by user through a Stop call.
+  Stopped
+  // Job has exited unexpectedly (for example due to invalid args, or permission denined while accessing a resource).
+  Exited
+  // Job has been terminated by service (likely due to OOMKiller).
+  Terminated
+)
+
+// Job status metadata including the process id, exit code if process exited, execution start time, execution end time and flags to indicate whether the process was terminated, and/or whether it is still running.
+type JobStatus struct {
+  Pid int
+  ExitCode int
+  StartTime time.Time
+  EndTime time.Time
+  State JobState
+}
+
+// Job metadata model which holds information about owner, actual command and job status.
+type Job struct {
+  Owner          string
+  JobID          string
+  Command        string
+  Args           []string
+  Cmd            *exec.Cmd
+  StdoutBuffer   OutputStream
+  StderrBuffer   OutputStream
+  CombinedBuffer OutputStream
+  Status         *JobStatus
+}
+```
+Note: the model is illustrative and might change slightly as the implementation evolves. 
+
+##### Stop Job
+
+Once a call is made to Executor to stop a job, it will validate the existence and the state of the job that's requested to be stopped, if the job doesn't exist we will return an error while if it's not running we will return a successful response. If the job exists and is in running state, then Executor will proceed to kill the job by interacting with the cgroup module to call ```KillJob()``` method which will utilizing the kill file feature from cgroups to kill all the processes running within the cgroup. After the job is killed successfully we will verify all the resources created for that job are throughly cleaned up and no resource is leaked or left behind. The other option would be to kill the process directly through the cmd object we are maintaining in our job metdata model which is equally going to SIGKILL the process. Though, using the cgroup method is going to be cleaner and easier especially when the job we are executing might start child processes, as that would require extra handling that we don't have to worry about with the ```cgroup.kill``` option.
+
+After stopping the job, Executor will still retain the job metadata information of the job but will discard the buffers that we have allocated for stdout, stderr through calling ```Close()``` on these buffers. It will also update the status of the job to indicate the job has been killed, and return the response to the client.
+
+Similarly during the service shutdown, it will be possible to kill all the running jobs by using the cgroup.kill file on the service/parent cgroup.
+
+##### Job Output Streaming
+
+During the execution of the job, Executor will initialize two memory buffers and redirect stdout and stderr of the process to the two buffers respectively, where a reference to those buffers will be maintained as part of the job metadata model in the in-memory map. Callers to the Executor's StreamOutput method will have initialize a channel and pass to the Executor in the input, and upon making a call to stream the output, we will initialize an outputStream object which will receive the requested memory buffer and the channel that the Caller passed in the input. This outputStream will be responsible for reading the content from the selected output buffer (whether that's stdout or stderr), and write the content of the buffer to the supplied channel. Caller (which is our API server in this case) will then read the data from the channel, and pass it over to the client using the grpc ```Send```. Output buffer will be implemented with mutex to ensure safety, it will also implement a mechanism to monitor the state of the buffer and block until new data to be written to the buffer or the buffer is closed.

+```
+// OutputStream is an interface representing a buffer implementation
+// that can store stdout, stderr and stream them out.
+type OutputStream interface {
+  sio.WriteCloser
+  sio.ReaderAt
+
+  Stream(dataChan chan []byte) error
+}
+
+// OutputBufferStream implements OutputStream.
+// It will hold output of the job/process being executed and Stream it when requested.
+type OutputBufferStream struct {
+  // internal buffer to hold the actual process output
+  buf      []byte
+  // closed is a boolean to indicate that buffer is closed
+  closed   bool
+  // mutex to ensure access safety.
+  *sync.RWMutex
+}
+```
+
+#### Control groups
+
+cgroup is the second core module in our library which will provide a wrapper around multiple cgroups v2 features, the module will be implemented to be self-contained and can be used separately from the rest of the library core modules.

+During the initialization of an Executor instance, it will interact with the cgroup module to make sure the requested controllers/subsystems are supported and enabled, then it will create a parent control group ```/sys/fs/cgroup/jws```, that will later hold the per-job child cgroups, so our hierarchy will look like:
+
+          ($root cgroup - /sys/fs/cgroup)
+                         |
+                         |
+           ($service cgroup - $root/jws)
+            /            |            \
+           /             |             \
+    ($service/job1) ($service/job2) ($server/job3) ...
+
+This hierarchy will allow us to control job's access to the resources in two ways, the first is by setting an upper limit for our different resources on the parent/service cgroup and let the different jobs compete for the resources depending on their need. While the second way is by limiting the job itself if the need arise.

+For simplicity we will cover only the following controls:
+- **Cpu:** we will support setting cpu time quota in ```cpu.max``` during one period.
+- **Memory:** we will support setting ```memory.high``` to throttle process's usage, and ```memory.max``` to set the upper boundry for which the process will OOMKilled if exceeded.

+message StopResponse {

+  int32 exit_code = 4;
+

+  string details = 6;
+}

+  // Server assigned id previously returned in response to a Start call.
+  string job_id = 1;

+# Job Worker Service
+
+## What
+
+A prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Details
+
+### High-level design
+
+![high-level design](assets/jws.jpg)
+
+To build our service with scalability in mind, we would need to design the service in such a way that makes it possible to scale every component in our service separately
+
+#### Control Plane
+
+Control plane will represent our customer facing API, which can either be an API GW, or a load balancer, and a cluster of containers behind it to process client requests. This control plane will be responsible for the following tasks:
+
+- Provide an API for data plane agents to register: agents will be installed and started on a fleet of hosts in data plane. They will need to register themselves with our control plane using a pre-configured api key.
+- Monitor the registered agents with heartbeats: Upon registering an agent in our control plane, the agent will start sending heartbeats to the control plane over a specific interval to allow making decision as to when our control plane should backoff on sending traffic to the agent if/when it's busy. These heartbeats can also be used to monitor the state of the jobs that the agent has been assigned.
+- Authenticate clients and process job requests: Once a client request is authenticated in our control plane using mTLS, the request will be routed by our control plane to an appropriate agent for execution.
+- Add a record about the job in a persistent external datastore: After re-routing the job to an agent, control plane will insert a record to a datastore (such as DynamoDB). This record will include metadata about the job that's being executed, the identifier of the agent that it was assigned to, and the state of the job.
+- Update the state of the job in the datastore: based on the heartbeats received from the agent, our control plane will update the state of the jobs that the agent was assigned accordingly.
+
+This persistent datastore will allow any container in our control plane cluster to respond to client requests belonging to any job and idenfiy which agent the job is running on when needed, as well as handling service restarts.
+
+#### Data Plane
+
+Data plane will consist of fleet of hosts that will be managed by an agent. Ideally, this fleet can be owned and provided by the client themself in case of sophisticated systems with high traffic, especially where multi-tenancy is not an option. Though a limited service fleet can be built to accommodate simple client requests. The agent will expose an internal API which should only be accessible by our control plane. This API will be used by our control plane to submit new jobs to the agent, query, or request the output stream of any given job. Agent will track the jobs that it has been assigned in memory.
+
+### Security
+
+The reason to separate out the execution environment (where the jobs are executed) from the rest of our service components is not just to achieve scalability, but also because - and due to the nature of our service - this execution environment is meant to be an untrusted environment. That means, the execution environment needs to be an isolated environment that doesn't handle any credentials or sensitive information, and is not allowed access to any other components in our service or infrastructure.
+
+Other general security considerations include:
+- All client-server and inter-service communications are sent over TLS.
+- A basic client authn/authz scheme is implemented over mTLS.
+- TLSv1.3 is used with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 cipher.
+- Resource isolation will be implemented to make sure each job is executed in a separate Pid namespace, network namespace and mount namespace.
+- Control groups will be used to control how much resource each job can access.
+
+A future improvement could be to implement a seccomp filter and limit access to the kernel and syscalls that a job can make. Linux capabilities can also be used to control what capabilities any job/process will have.
+

+
+As the purpose of this project is to prototype our service only, we are going to limit the scope to include only the data plane agent in standalone mode, where it will be possible to send the requests directly to the agent's API, and the agent will handle the client authn/authz instead. +
+- A reusable library implementing the functionality for working with jobs.
+- An API server that wraps the functionality of the library.
+- A command line interface (CLI) that communicates with the API server.
+
+### Protobuf Definition
+

+}

+}

+  // Server assigned id previously returned in response to a Start call.

+}

+  // nothing to return in successful case.
+}

+  // Server assigned id previously returned in response to a Start call.
+  string job_id = 1;
+

+}

+  // Unknown status.
+  JOB_STATUS_UNKNOWN = 0
+
+  // Job is running.
+  RUNNING = 1;
+
+  // Job completed successfully.
+  COMPLETED = 2;
+
+  // Job has been stopped in response to a Stop call.
+  STOPPED = 3;
+
+  // Job exited unexpectedly.
+  EXITED = 4;

+  int32 exit_code = 4;

+  // Optional string to capture additional details or cause of termination.
+  string details = 6;
+}

+### Authentication and Authorization
+

+
+Our authz model will involve mapping the organisation a user belongs to (as embedded into the certificate) to an access role with a very simple RBAC (Role-based access control). For simplicity we are going to support only the following organizational groups in our prototype:
+
+- **Users:** each user in this organizational group will have permissions to submit new jobs, stop, request the output or query the status of *their own jobs only*.
+- **Admins:** each user in this organizational group will have permissions to submit new jobs, stop, request the output or query the status of *any* job (provided that they have the job id for that job).
+
+Ideally, we would have a Roles table in our dynamodb in control plane were we could define the privileges and permissions of every organizational group to support more sophisticated RBAC.
+A further API endpoint can be implemented to allow Users to list their own jobs, and Admins to list all jobs on the service with pagination so that it's less important for them to maintain the job ids, but this is out of scope for this prototype.
+
+### Client CLI:
+
+A client command line tool that provides the interface represented below will be implemented:
+
+```
+usage: jws [options] <action> [parameters]
+
+actions:
+- start
+- stop
+- query
+- stream
+
+To see help text, you can run:
+
+  jws --help
+  jws <action> --help
+
+```
+
+
+### Open Questions
+
+Q: Do we want to allow clients to request certain resource limits for their job?
+A: In this prototype and as we are not building a scalable system, we won't allow the clients to set their desired resource limits. Though this can be a feature to add in a real-world implementation.

+# Job Worker Service
+
+## What
+
+A prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Details
+
+### High-level design
+
+![high-level design](assets/jws.jpg)
+
+To build our service with scalability in mind, we would need to design the service in such a way that makes it possible to scale every component in our service separately
+
+#### Control Plane
+
+Control plane will represent our customer facing API, which can either be an API GW, or a load balancer, and a cluster of containers behind it to process client requests. This control plane will be responsible for the following tasks:
+
+- Provide an API for data plane agents to register: agents will be installed and started on a fleet of hosts in data plane. They will need to register themselves with our control plane using a pre-configured api key.
+- Monitor the registered agents with heartbeats: Upon registering an agent in our control plane, the agent will start sending heartbeats to the control plane over a specific interval to allow making decision as to when our control plane should backoff on sending traffic to the agent if/when it's busy. These heartbeats can also be used to monitor the state of the jobs that the agent has been assigned.
+- Authenticate clients and process job requests: Once a client request is authenticated in our control plane using mTLS, the request will be routed by our control plane to an appropriate agent for execution.
+- Add a record about the job in a persistent external datastore: After re-routing the job to an agent, control plane will insert a record to a datastore (such as DynamoDB). This record will include metadata about the job that's being executed, the identifier of the agent that it was assigned to, and the state of the job.
+- Update the state of the job in the datastore: based on the heartbeats received from the agent, our control plane will update the state of the jobs that the agent was assigned accordingly.
+
+This persistent datastore will allow any container in our control plane cluster to respond to client requests belonging to any job and idenfiy which agent the job is running on when needed, as well as handling service restarts.
+
+#### Data Plane
+
+Data plane will consist of fleet of hosts that will be managed by an agent. Ideally, this fleet can be owned and provided by the client themself in case of sophisticated systems with high traffic, especially where multi-tenancy is not an option. Though a limited service fleet can be built to accommodate simple client requests. The agent will expose an internal API which should only be accessible by our control plane. This API will be used by our control plane to submit new jobs to the agent, query, or request the output stream of any given job. Agent will track the jobs that it has been assigned in memory.
+
+### Security
+
+The reason to separate out the execution environment (where the jobs are executed) from the rest of our service components is not just to achieve scalability, but also because - and due to the nature of our service - this execution environment is meant to be an untrusted environment. That means, the execution environment needs to be an isolated environment that doesn't handle any credentials or sensitive information, and is not allowed access to any other components in our service or infrastructure.
+
+Other general security considerations include:
+- All client-server and inter-service communications are sent over TLS.
+- A basic client authn/authz scheme is implemented over mTLS.
+- TLSv1.3 is used with TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 cipher.
+- Resource isolation will be implemented to make sure each job is executed in a separate Pid namespace, network namespace and mount namespace.
+- Control groups will be used to control how much resource each job can access.

+# Job Worker Service
+
+## What
+
+A prototype job worker service that provides an API to run arbitrary Linux processes.
+
+## Details
+
+### Scope
+
+We will implement a grpc API server with a backend library that allows clients to execute arbitrary Linux processes on a remote host. Our API server will expose the following API endpoints /Start, /Stop, /Query, and /Stream which are going to allow clients to start a process, stop a process, query to status of a process, and request the output stream of a process. Our project can be broken down into 3 components:
+
+- A reusable library implementing the functionality for working with jobs.
+- An API server that wraps the functionality of the library.
+- A command line interface (CLI) that communicates with the API server.
+
+### Library
+
+Our backend library will expose an interface that allows our API server to interact with the library and perform actions that correspond to each API endpoint. The implemented interface will be portable and will not be tied to our grpc server use-case, allowing other programs which might be looking to adapt any of the existing functionality to integrate easily with the library.
+
+#### Executor
+Executor is the main component in our library which will be responsible for the core business logic of executing, stopping, tracking the status, and streaming output of a process.
+
+##### Start Job
+For every new job started by Executor, a unique job identifier (a uuid string) will be generated which can be used by users of the library to perform actions on that particular job referencing its id. Following the generation of the job id, we will create a separate control group for the new job, execute the provided command and add the process id to the created control group. Executor will make sure that every command is executed in its own separate pid, network and mount namespaces.
+
+In order to make sure the process is executed in an isolated and controlled environment from the get-go, the execution flow for each job will involve the following steps:
+- **Control group creation:** We will create a cgroup for the job, we are going to have a 1:1 mapping between the cgroup and job, and make sure it has cpu, cpuset, memory and io controllers enabled, at this step the created cgroup will have no process in it.
+- **Entrypoint execution:** We are going to implement a simple cmd ```entrypoint``` which will be responsible for executing the provided command inside the isolated environment. A pid, network, and mount namespaces will be initialized as part of this step. Once the entrypoint is started, we will add its process id to our previously created cgroup for the particular job, this entrypoint cmd will prepare a pivot root in which the job or the command provided will be executed before proceeding to executing the job's command.
+- **Job execution:** we will pass the provided command along with its arguments to our entrypoint script which will subsequently execute the command after it has completed preparing the isolated environment. The job's command will be then executed using ```syscall.Exec``` to replace the current process with the command itself allowing the new process to become the init inside our pid namespace.
+- **Record job information:** Once the command is executed successfully, Executor will add an entry to an in-memory map while holding a mutex to ensure safety. This map maintains information about every job it's executed, where the key of this map the job id, and the value is a job metadata model that will hold the information represented below.
+- **Wait for job to complete or exit:** Executor and after it has stored the job information in the in-memory map, it will call ```Wait()``` on the started command in order to wait for the process to exit.
+
+```
+// Job status metadata including the process id, exit code if process exited, execution start time, execution end time and flags to indicate whether the process was terminated, and/or whether it is still running.
+type JobStatus struct {
+  Pid int
+  ExitCode int
+  StartTime string
+  EndTime string
+  IsKilled bool
+  IsRunning bool
+}
+
+// Job metadata model which holds information about owner, actual command and job status.
+type Job struct {
+  Owner         string
+  JobID         uuid.UUID
+  Command       string
+  Args          []string
+  Cmd           *exec.Cmd
+  StdoutBuffer  io.Writer
+  StderrBuffer  io.Writer
+  Status        *JobStatus
+}
+```
+Note: the model is illustrative and might change slightly as the implementation evolves. 
+
+##### Stop Job
+
+Once a call is made to Executor to stop a job, it will validate the existence and the state of the job that's requested to be stopped, if the job doesn't exist we will return an error while if it's not running we will return a successful response. If the job exists and is in running state, then Executor will proceed to kill the job by interacting with the cgroup module to call ```KillJob()``` method which will utilizing the kill file feature from cgroups to kill all the processes running within the cgroup. After the job is killed successfully we will verify all the resources created for that job are throughly cleaned up and no resource is leaked or left bihind.
+
+After stopping the job, Executor will still retain the job metadata information of the job as well as the output buffers created for stdout/stderr of the job in memory, but will update the status of the job to indicate the job has been killed, and return the response to the client.

comment.body:
The purpose of entrypoint is to setup the pivot root which has to be setup inside the mount namespace, so instead of executing the command we received from the API directly, we would be executing using it through the entrypoint binary, for example:

```
...
cmd := exec.Command("entrypoint", jobArgs...)
// set stdout and stderr to their respective buffers
cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{
   Cloneflags: syscall.CLONE_NEWNS,
}
...
if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
   // log and return an error
}
```

where entrypoint is essentially going to do the following:
- create a newRoot
- bind mount it to itself
- create a directory for oldRoot
- call ```syscall.PivotRoot(newRoot, oldRoot)```
- call ```syscall.Chdir("/")```
- execute the job's command by calling ```syscall.Exec(args[0], args)```

I'm not aware of another way to setup the pivot root in such a use-case, unless we use a chroot only instead of a pivot root, but chroot isn't secure and is easy to escape.

+- Add a record about the job in a persistent external datastore: After re-routing the job to an agent, control plane will insert a record to a datastore (such as DynamoDB). +

+
+Data plane will consist of fleet of hosts that will be managed by an agent. +- Control groups will be used to control how much resource each job can access.
